claims: A market schedule records quantities demanded and supplied at stated prices during a stated period.
With other relevant conditions unchanged, a change in the product’s own price causes movements along its demand and supply curves rather than shifts.
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied for the stated period.
A price below equilibrium creates excess demand in the basic model, while a price above equilibrium creates excess supply.
An increase in demand means buyers are willing and able to buy more at each price, shifting demand to the right.
An increase in supply shifts supply to the right and, with demand unchanged in the basic model, lowers equilibrium price and raises equilibrium quantity.
A non-price determinant changes demand or supply at given prices, rather than moving along the existing curve because the product’s own price changes.
Income, tastes, population and prices of related goods can affect demand; production costs, technology, weather and producer numbers can affect supply.
Substitutes are alternative products meeting a similar want; a brand and the category containing it are not two distinct alternatives.
Demand shifts concern quantities at given prices, while price elasticity concerns responsiveness of quantity demanded to the product’s price change.
Excess demand is the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a stated price.
Higher demand with supply unchanged tends to raise equilibrium price and quantity; lower supply with demand unchanged tends to raise price and lower quantity.
The quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged, constitute demand.
A desire without the willingness and ability to pay is not effective demand.
The quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged, constitute supply.
Supply is a planned flow over a period and is distinct from the stock physically held at a point in time.
A controlled price is represented as a price level relative to the existing curves; imposing it alone does not shift demand or supply.
When demand and supply both change, the effect on equilibrium price or quantity can be uncertain without information about their relative changes.

CU-6145-3.2:
Demand and supply schedules describe planned purchases and sales at different prices during a stated period. Quantities need units and a time period: packets per week differs from packets held in a storeroom. A demand curve shows the buyer relationship and a supply curve the producer relationship. Conventionally put price on the vertical axis and quantity per period on the horizontal axis. Label the curves D and S, attach units to the axes and use one consistent scale. Each plotted point is a price-quantity pair, not an arbitrary mark on the page.

For an original market in seed packets, use prices N$10, N$20 and N$30 per packet. Quantities demanded per week are respectively 90, 60 and 30; quantities supplied are 30, 60 and 90. Plot demand coordinates as (quantity, price): (90,10), (60,20), (30,30). Supply points are (30,10), (60,20), (90,30). Join each set with a straight line for this simple example. Demand slopes down and supply slopes up. The data are illustrative relationships, not a claim about every real market. Moving from N$10 to N$20 along these schedules reduces quantity demanded and increases quantity supplied while other relevant conditions remain unchanged.

Check the placement of coordinates before joining points. At a price of N$10, the demand quantity 90 belongs at horizontal coordinate 90 and vertical coordinate 10. Reversing the axes while leaving the labels unchanged would misrepresent the schedule. The supply point at that same price is at horizontal coordinate 30. The horizontal distance between them therefore represents a quantity difference at one price. A vertical distance instead represents a price difference at one quantity. Reading the units makes these two comparisons easier to keep separate.

Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. In the seed-packet schedule it is N$20, where both equal 60 packets per week. Mark the intersection E, then project to the axes to show the equilibrium price and quantity. Equality matters: a high quantity or a price acceptable to one trader alone does not establish equilibrium. Equilibrium also does not mean every consumer obtains all they would like at no cost; it concerns planned quantities at the stated market price.

At N$10, buyers want 90 packets while sellers offer 30, producing excess demand of 60 packets per week. Competition for limited offers can put upward pressure on price. As price rises along unchanged curves, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises. At N$30, supply of 90 exceeds demand of 30, leaving excess supply of 60 and downward pressure on price. In the basic model prices can adjust towards N$20. Real adjustment may take time, and regulation or contractual arrangements can prevent free movement. A controlled price below equilibrium would be drawn as a horizontal price line below E, not as a new demand curve. Price control changes the permitted price; its imposition alone does not establish that buyers’ tastes or producers’ costs changed.

A movement along a curve follows a change in the product’s own price, other relevant conditions unchanged. A shift follows a change in another determinant, so the quantity at a given price changes. Higher income may raise demand for a normal good; changes in preferences, population and related-product prices can also shift demand. The direction depends on the relationship. If tea and an invented herbal drink are substitutes, a higher tea price may increase demand for the herbal drink. If two products are used together, a higher price of one can reduce demand for the other. Name two distinct alternatives when giving a substitute pair: a named type of bread and bread as its whole category do not provide two separate alternatives.

Supply determinants concern producers’ willingness and ability to offer output. Higher input costs can reduce supply, while improved technology can increase it. Weather can affect agricultural output, and entry or exit of producers can change market supply. Explain the channel rather than assigning a factor by its name alone. A household income change directly concerns buyers; a rise in the cost of cloth concerns suppliers of clothing. Demand-shift factors also differ from determinants of price responsiveness. The availability of close substitutes helps explain responsiveness to a product’s own price; a change in tastes can instead move the entire demand curve. Responsiveness is developed in topic 3.3, so do not treat a shift as evidence that elasticity has increased.

When the term price elasticity is used, its consequential forms include elastic, inelastic, unit elastic and perfectly inelastic demand. These describe responsiveness, not a choice between a rightward and a leftward shift. Their definitions and calculations belong to topic 3.3. A change in tastes alone does not supply the price-and-quantity evidence needed to select a responsiveness category. Holding the distinction clear here prevents the same word change being used for two different analytical questions.

Keep the original seed-packet supply schedule. Now suppose more households begin home gardening, and demand at N$10, N$20 and N$30 becomes 120, 90 and 60 packets per week. Plot the new demand curve D1 through (120,10), (90,20), (60,30), to the right of D0. At the old N$20 price, demand is now 90 but supply remains 60, so excess demand is 30. This puts upward pressure on price if it can adjust. The new intersection lies at N$25 and 75 packets per week: on the straight-line schedules, demand and supply both equal 75 there.

Show E0 at (60,20) and E1 at (75,25), with axis projections for both. Demand has shifted, but the price adjustment creates a movement along the unchanged supply curve. It would be wrong to shift supply simply because producers offer more at the higher price. The new equilibrium has both higher price and higher quantity because buyers demand more at each price while the supply relationship is unchanged. The direction can be explained without calculating a slope: compare the old and new curves, identify the imbalance at the old price, then trace the adjustment towards the new intersection.
A supply change and competing effects

Return to the original demand curve and consider improved production methods that raise supply by 30 packets at each listed price. New supply at N$10, N$20 and N$30 is 60, 90 and 120. Plot S1 to the right of S0. At the old N$20 price, supply is 90 and demand is 60, leaving excess supply of 30. Price tends downwards; the new equilibrium is N$15 and 75 packets per week. This is a supply increase, not a reduction, because more is offered at the same price. The demand curve stays in place while quantity demanded rises along it as price falls.

A supply reduction works in the opposite direction: with demand unchanged, price tends to rise and equilibrium quantity to fall. If both demand and supply increase, quantity rises in the basic model but the direction of price depends on the relative shifts. Stronger demand pushes price upwards, while stronger supply pushes it downwards. Without magnitudes, a definite net price claim would be unsupported. This gives a useful analysis sequence: identify the affected side and determinant, state the shift, compare quantities at the old price, then locate the new equilibrium. Connect this reasoning to productivity in topic 5.2 for production changes and to advertising in topic 3.4 for changes in buyer information or preferences. A diagram supports the mechanism only when its labels, direction and written conclusion agree.

A price rise and a quantity fall together are consistent with a supply reduction when demand is unchanged. A price rise and a quantity rise are consistent with a demand increase when supply is unchanged. These comparisons help interpret a supplied case, but observations alone do not prove the unchanged conditions. A real event may affect both sides. For example, a local festival may attract more buyers while temporary transport problems restrict deliveries. Explain both changes if the case supplies them, then state what additional information is needed for a definite net conclusion. Do not use the convenience of a simple diagram to erase a stated second change. A conclusion should state the comparison explicitly: price relative to the original equilibrium, quantity relative to the original equilibrium, and which conditions were held unchanged. This keeps a correct curve shift connected to its economic meaning.
CU-6145-3.2.1: Demand is willing and able buying

Demand means the quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged. Wanting an expensive product without the ability to pay does not constitute effective demand at that price. Ability alone is also insufficient if the person chooses not to buy. The definition brings willingness and ability together. State the period because buying ten loaves each week differs from buying ten loaves each month.

A demand schedule describes several possible quantities at different prices, rather than a single purchase. In a simple example, an invented household buys six packets per month at N$12 each but four at N$18, with its income and preferences unchanged. That is a movement between quantities on the same demand relationship. If a change in the household’s circumstances causes it to buy more at both prices, the relationship itself has changed. This distinction avoids saying demand increased merely because a lower price encouraged a larger purchase. For a market, the quantities bought by relevant buyers can be combined at each price. Do not add quantities referring to different prices as though they were simultaneous purchases at one market price. The curve is a set of alternatives under stated conditions, not a pile of quantities to be summed across the price axis.

The willingness-and-ability test also explains why a survey of wishes is not a complete demand schedule. Respondents might like a product while being unable or unwilling to purchase it at the listed price. A useful schedule specifies the product, price, quantity and period under relevant conditions. It can concern one buyer or a whole market, so state which is meant before interpreting a quantity. A change in market buyer numbers can alter market demand even if each existing buyer’s schedule is unchanged.

Supply means the quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged. A producer might possess inputs but lack the capacity to produce more immediately. It might also hold output but choose not to offer all of it at the current price. Supply therefore concerns planned offers under stated conditions, rather than physical stock alone. An existing inventory records what is held at a point in time; weekly supply records a flow offered during a period.

For an invented soap workshop, a higher selling price may make additional weekly output worthwhile, provided inputs and capacity allow it. The workshop moves along its existing supply curve when its own product price changes and other relevant conditions stay the same. If a new process reduces the resources needed per bar, more may be offered at each price, shifting supply. The words more output are insufficient to distinguish the two cases: explain why the planned quantity changes. A seller choosing an asking price does not establish that buyers will purchase the entire offer. Demand and supply are separate plans, and their equality identifies equilibrium in the main unit. This links the member definitions back to the market diagram: price belongs on the vertical axis, quantities per period on the horizontal axis, and the labels identify buyer or producer plans rather than actual sales assumed in advance.

Capacity matters when interpreting producers’ plans. Higher prices can encourage more output, but a workshop already using its equipment fully may be unable to respond quickly. This does not change the definition of supply; it shows why the time period and production conditions belong in the explanation. Stocks can help a seller meet current orders, while future supply may depend on replenishment or new production. Avoid treating goods sitting in storage as necessarily offered for sale at every possible price.

cards: Define a market schedule for demand and supply.
A record of quantities demanded and supplied at stated prices over a stated period.
Definition: price-quantity record, 1; qualifier: planned buying/selling over a period, 1.

Use these data to draw original demand and supply curves: price N$8, N$12, N$16; weekly demand 80,60,40 units; weekly supply 40,60,80. Put quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. Show the change along both curves when price rises from N$8 to N$16 (4).

Plot D through (80,8),(60,12),(40,16) and S through (40,8),(60,12),(80,16). Label price N$ per unit vertically and units per week horizontally. D slopes down, S up; arrows run up-left on D and up-right on S for the stated price rise.
Diagram: axes/labels 1, original D points/line 1, original S points/line 1, change arrows along existing curves 1.

Explain the relationship in a market schedule where price rises from N$6 to N$9, quantity demanded falls from 70 to 50 and quantity supplied rises from 30 to 50 units per week, other conditions unchanged.

Demand has a negative price relationship while supply has a positive one. Buyers plan 20 fewer units and producers 20 more. The changes are movements along existing curves because the product’s own price changes with other conditions fixed. At N$9 both planned quantities are 50.
Relationship: opposite demand/supply directions 1; evidence: stated quantities 1; explanation: own-price movements, not shifts 2.
Explain why a lower price of an invented snack causing more purchases, with income and tastes unchanged, is not a demand-curve shift.
The snack’s own price changed (1), so the greater quantity is a movement along the existing demand curve (1).
Context: snack; reasoning: own-price change 1; result: movement rather than shift 1.
Define equilibrium price.
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied over the stated period.
Meaning: market price 1; distinguishing feature: equality of planned quantities 1.

Use a diagram to show equilibrium for weekly demand points (quantity, price): (90,10),(60,20),(30,30), and supply points (30,10),(60,20),(90,30). Prices are N$ per packet. Mark the change towards equilibrium from N$10 (4).

Draw labelled D and S on quantity-per-week and N$-price axes. The original intersection E is (60,20); project N$20 and 60 onto the axes. At N$10 mark Qs 30 and Qd 90, excess demand 60; show upward price adjustment towards N$20.
Diagram labels/axes 1; original curves 1; E and projections 1; change from shortage with upward adjustment 1.
Explain what happens at a price of N$30 when demand is 30 and supply is 90 packets per week, while at N$20 both are 60. Assume price can adjust.

At N$30 there is excess supply of 60 packets per week. Sellers face offers greater than planned purchases, putting downward pressure on price. As it falls along unchanged curves, demand quantity rises and supply quantity falls. N$20 is equilibrium because both quantities equal 60 there.
Relationship: excess supply 1; evidence: 90 minus 30 equals 60, with equilibrium equality 1; explanation: downward adjustment and movements 2.
Explain why 100 units offered and 65 units wanted at a price of N$40 do not show equilibrium.
Supply exceeds demand by 35 units (1), so the planned quantities are unequal rather than in equilibrium (1).
Context: offers versus wants; reasoning: excess supply 1; result: not equilibrium 1.
Define an increase in demand.
An increase in quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at each price, shown by a rightward demand shift.
Definition: more at each price 1; qualifier: demand relationship shifts right 1.

Use a diagram for seed packets to show an increase in demand. Original weekly demand at N$10,20,30 is 90,60,30; new demand is 120,90,60; unchanged supply is 30,60,90. Use straight lines and label both equilibria (4).

Plot D0 through (90,10),(60,20),(30,30); D1 through (120,10),(90,20),(60,30); S through (30,10),(60,20),(90,30). Label E0=(60,20), E1=(75,25), and projections. D1 is right of D0; price rises N$20 to N$25 and quantity 60 to 75.
Diagram labels/axes 1; original D0/S 1; demand change D1 rightward 1; equilibria/projections 1.
Explain the effect of an increase in supply where the old equilibrium is N$20 and 60 packets weekly, and the new equilibrium is N$15 and 75 with demand unchanged.

The supply curve shifts right, meaning more offered at given prices. At the old price the extra offers create excess supply, pushing price down. The new equilibrium price is N$5 lower and quantity 15 packets higher; buyers move along unchanged demand.
Relationship: supply rightward 1; evidence: price/quantity changes 1; explanation: excess supply and movement along demand 2.
Explain the likely market effect of improved production technology for an invented cup maker when demand is unchanged.
Lower production difficulty or cost allows more cups to be offered at each price (1), so supply shifts right, tending to lower equilibrium price and raise quantity (1).
Context: cup production; reasoning: more at each price 1; result: supply increase effects 1.
Define a non-price determinant of demand or supply.
A factor other than the product’s own price that changes quantities demanded or supplied at given prices.
Meaning: factor other than own price 1; qualifier: changes relationship at given prices 1.
Explain how higher cloth costs can affect the supply of shirts.
Initial change: cloth costs rise (1); producing shirts becomes more costly for the firm, reducing the amount it is willing to offer at each price (1).
Initial change: input cost rise 1; mechanism/effect for firm: reduced supply at given prices 1.
Explain how a rise in the price of tea may affect demand for an invented herbal drink if the drinks are substitutes.
Tea becomes relatively more expensive (1), so some buyers may switch to the herbal drink, raising its demand at given prices (1).
Context: substitute drinks; reasoning: relative price encourages switching 1; result: herbal-drink demand increases 1.
Define excess demand.
The amount by which quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a stated price.
Definition: demand quantity greater than supply 1; qualifier: difference at stated price 1.

Use a diagram to show a supply increase with unchanged weekly demand. At N$10,20,30 demand is 90,60,30; original supply is 30,60,90 and new supply 60,90,120. Label the original and changed equilibria (4).

Draw D unchanged; S0 through (30,10),(60,20),(90,30); S1 through (60,10),(90,20),(120,30). The supply change is rightward. E0=(60,20); E1=(75,15). Show N$20 falling to N$15 and weekly quantity 60 rising to 75 using projections.
Diagram axes/labels 1; original D/S0 1; change S1 rightward 1; equilibria and projections 1.
Explain why a market experiencing both higher demand and higher supply cannot be assigned a definite new price without more information.

Higher demand tends to push price up; higher supply tends to push it down. The opposing influences mean their relative size determines the net price effect. For example, a large demand increase with a small supply increase can raise price, while the reverse can lower it.
Relationship: opposing price pressures 1; evidence: explicit contrasting relative-shift examples 1; explanation: net effect requires magnitude information 2.
Explain the effect of a crop failure reducing vegetable supply when demand is unchanged.
Less is offered at each price (1), so the supply reduction tends to raise equilibrium price and lower equilibrium quantity (1).
Context: crop failure; reasoning: leftward supply change 1; result: price up/quantity down 1.
Define demand.
The quantities buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged.
Definition: willing and able buying 1; qualifier: price range/period with other conditions unchanged 1.
Define supply.
The quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period, other relevant conditions unchanged.
Meaning: willing and able offering 1; qualifier: prices/period with other conditions unchanged 1.
Explain the error in treating a rise in household income as an increase in producers’ supply merely because households buy more.

The change directly affects buyers’ willingness and ability to purchase (1), so for a normal good it shifts demand; higher production following a price response is not itself proof of a supply shift (1).
Confusion: buyer versus producer determinant; boundary/test: quantities at given prices, 1 each.
Explain the error in showing a price ceiling alone as a leftward shift of demand.
The control specifies a permitted price rather than changing quantities buyers want at each price (1), so it is shown as a horizontal price level against the existing curves (1).
Confusion: price rule versus curve determinant; boundary/test: permitted price line versus changed relationship, 1 each.
Explain why an invented brand of maize meal and maize meal as a whole are not a clear pair of substitutes.
The brand belongs inside the product category (1); a substitute pair needs distinct alternatives, such as maize meal and another staple used instead (1).
Confusion: member/category mistaken for alternatives; boundary/test: two separate replacement choices, 1 each.
Explain why greater demand after a change in tastes is not, by itself, evidence of greater price elasticity.
Tastes can change quantities wanted at given prices, shifting demand (1); elasticity concerns quantity responsiveness to the product’s own price, which this fact does not measure (1).
Confusion: shift versus responsiveness; boundary/test: given-price change versus own-price response, 1 each.
performance: At the invented Sandridge seed market, weekly prices N$10,20,30 correspond to demand of 90,60,30 packets and supply of 30,60,90. A gardening campaign increases demand to 120,90,60 at those prices, with supply unchanged. Assume straight lines and flexible prices. (a) Describe three features of the original schedules (6). (b) Examine the effect of the campaign on equilibrium (7). (c) Suggest how traders should interpret the higher price before planning stock (7).

(a) Demand falls by 30 packets for each N$10 price increase. Supply rises by 30. Original equilibrium is N$20 and 60 packets because plans are equal. (b) Demand shifts right by 30 packets at each price. At N$20 there is excess demand of 30, creating upward price pressure. The new intersection is N$25 and 75 packets weekly. Supply has not shifted: producers move along it as price rises. (c) Traders should treat the change as evidence of higher demand, not lower supply. Planning may allow for 75 rather than 60 packets under the stated model, but an individual trader should not assume it supplies the whole market. Check whether the campaign effect persists and whether its own capacity fits the extra sales. A temporary campaign or other changing conditions could make the estimated new equilibrium short-lived; the judgement depends on continuing demand and unchanged supply conditions.

Context: Sandridge. Parts/allocation: (a) demand pattern 2, supply pattern 2, equality 2 = 6. (b) shift 2, excess-demand mechanism 2, new equilibrium 2, movement along S 1 = 7. (c) correct interpretation 2, market-versus-firm distinction 2, conditional stock judgement and persistence 3 = 7.

(a) Define equilibrium price (2). (b) Explain why an own-price change need not shift demand (2). (c) Explain one demand determinant unrelated to own price (2). (d) Explain one supply determinant unrelated to own price (2). (e) Explain why a brand and its containing product category are not a distinct substitute pair (2). (f) Explain what excess supply means (2). (g) Explain why imposing a price level alone does not move the curves (2). (h) Explain why simultaneous demand and supply increases leave the net price direction uncertain without magnitudes (2).

(a) Price where quantities demanded and supplied are equal. (b) It changes quantity along the existing relationship, other conditions fixed. (c) Higher income can raise demand for a normal good by supporting purchases at given prices. (d) Lower input costs can increase planned offers at given prices. (e) One is contained in the other rather than being a distinct replacement product. (f) Supply quantity exceeds demand quantity at the stated price, leaving excess offers. (g) A rule about price does not itself change buyers’ or sellers’ quantities at every given price. (h) The shifts push price in opposite directions, so relative size matters.

Parts/allocation and precision: eight 2-mark parts. (a) price + quantity equality; (b) own price + movement; (c) buyer factor + given-price effect; (d) producer factor + given-price effect; (e) category membership + missing distinct alternatives; (f) excess quantity + stated price; (g) rule/relationship distinction; (h) opposing influences + relative magnitudes.

At an invented vegetable market, bad weather reduces quantities growers can supply at each price. Buyers’ incomes and preferences are unchanged. Initially price was N$12 per bundle and equilibrium quantity 200 bundles weekly. No new schedule or size of the supply reduction is supplied. (a) Define supply (2). (b) Explain two distinctions needed to analyse the event (4). (c) Explain the effect on the market using a labelled demand-and-supply diagram (7). (d) Discuss whether a trader can conclude that total weekly sales receipts must rise (7).

(a) Quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a period, other conditions unchanged. (b) Weather changes quantities at given prices, shifting supply rather than causing an own-price movement. Buyers’ conditions are unchanged, so demand stays in place even though quantity demanded changes with price. (c) Draw downward D and upward S0, label E0 and initial price N$12/quantity 200. Shift S left to S1. At the old price demand exceeds the reduced offer, tending to raise price. E1 has higher price and lower quantity; label projections but do not invent figures. (d) Each bundle sells at a higher price, tending to raise receipts per unit, but fewer bundles are sold, tending to reduce receipts. Without the size of each change, total price-times-quantity receipts cannot be established. A trader also needs its own quantity rather than treating the market as its business. The defensible judgement is that total receipts are uncertain, even though the direction of market price is clear.

Context: vegetable market. Parts/allocation: (a) producer willingness/ability 1, price/period qualifier 1. (b) two distinctions, each contrast + reason 2 = 4. (c) diagram labels/original 2, leftward change 1, shortage mechanism 2, new P/Q directions 2 = 7. (d) higher-price influence 2, lower-quantity influence 2, judgement avoiding unsupported magnitude and market/firm inference 3 = 7.

Evaluate whether a higher observed price is enough evidence for an invented local food supplier to conclude demand has increased, when no information on quantities or production conditions is supplied (9).

For: higher demand with unchanged supply would raise equilibrium price, so the observation is consistent with a demand increase. Against: a supply reduction with unchanged demand would also raise price but reduce quantity. Both sides may change, and relative shifts matter. A price observation alone cannot identify which determinant moved or establish the quantity effect. Judgement: obtain evidence about quantities, buyer circumstances and producer costs before assigning the cause. The condition for the simple demand explanation is credible evidence that supply conditions were unchanged and buyers wanted more at given prices. The higher price alone does not meet that condition.

Argument for: demand-shift mechanism with unchanged supply, up to 4. Argument against: alternative supply mechanism and simultaneous changes, up to 4. Judgement: distinct evidence condition, 1. Total 9.
judgements: Construction prompts supply complete original coordinate data for learners to plot; numerical geometry is checked independently in coordinate-audit.json. No generic break-even check is claimed as validation of demand/supply geometry.
Diagram slots use PROC exactly as planned. Parent DEF anchors use market schedule, demand increase, non-price determinant and excess demand rather than duplicate child definitions.
Price controls are distinguished briefly as required by MISCON-010; policy evaluation remains in theme 6.
